clue.text: Block essentially tackled by drain cleaner

indicators.note: The essence of a word sits at its very core, so a five-letter word is asked for its single middle letter.

parts.note: to sap something is to drain it of strength, and the word opens up to take a letter

indicators.note: A tackle closes right round the player being tackled, so whatever does the tackling wraps itself about the letter.

parts.note: the letter at the centre of blOck

explanation.surface: Something blocking a drain, and the stuff poured down the pipe to shift it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' looks like the thing stuck in the pipe and is really a word being cut down to one letter, while 'drain' is a verb rather than the pipe itself.
explanation.definitionFit: cleaner → SOAP: the plainest sense of the word, the household agent that lathers up and takes dirt off.

clue.text: Packed lunch from dodgy old Spar

parts.note: someone bent is crooked or dishonest, as in a bent copper
o is the standard short form of old
to spar is to box, trading practice punches

explanation.surface: A dubious lunch bought from a corner shop that has seen better days.
explanation.walkthrough: Spar is a chain of British convenience stores, which is what the capital letter is there to suggest; the word is really doing service as the boxers' verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Packed lunch → BENTO BOX: the Japanese compartmented lunch container, rice and fish packed into its trays, is a packed lunch exactly.

clue.text: Honey bee swallowed by horse

indicators.note: Anything swallowed disappears inside the swallower, so the letter ends up in the middle of the word that eats it.

parts.note: a bay is a reddish-brown horse
the insect is the name of the letter said aloud, so it stands for that single character

explanation.surface: A bee getting itself swallowed by a grazing horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Honey' is a term of endearment rather than the stuff bees make, and putting the insect right next to it keeps the hive in mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Honey → BABY: both are what you call someone you dote on, interchangeable as forms of address between fond adults.

clue.text: Aussie groundsmen stuck up schedule to feed dogs

indicators.note: to feed means to go into the mouths of, so the reversed schedule goes inside the dogs

parts.note: curs are mongrel dogs

indicators.note: stuck up in a down clue means placed upwards, so the schedule word is read from the bottom

parts.note: a rota is a schedule of duties

explanation.surface: A haughty timetable for feeding the hounds at an Australian ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuck up' looks like snobbish but turns ROTA into ATOR, which goes inside CURS.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian cricket the person who prepares the pitch is called the curator, the job a groundsman does elsewhere.

clue.text: Where you might see Neighbours actress not finishing on time

parts.note: Meryl Streep is the actress, halted before her closing letter
t is the standard short form of time

explanation.surface: An actress from the Australian soap turning up somewhere, and not quite finishing on time.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Neighbours a programme, and the show is set in Ramsay Street; with a small n the same word means the people living either side of you.
explanation.definitionFit: Where you might see Neighbours → STREET: the soap is set in one, and a street is literally where the people next door live.

clue.text: 1 tip to stop festival succeeded

indicators.note: To stop a gap is to plug it, so the piece named goes down into the middle of the word beside it.

parts.note: Easter is the festival, and it splits open to take another piece
the tip of a thing is its end
s is the genealogist's short form of succeeded

explanation.surface: A gratuity offered to bring a festival to a halt, and the bribe working.
explanation.walkthrough: The bare '1' sends you to 1-down, whose answer names a whole television genre, so the definition here is an example of that genre rather than a synonym for anything.
explanation.definitionFit: 1 → EASTENDERS: the answer at 1-down is the word for a television serial, and this long-running BBC one is an instance of it.

clue.text: Snow leopard finally cutting teeth

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the letter goes inside the word for teeth

parts.note: teeth means power or force, as in a law with real teeth

indicators.note: finally means take the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: leopard ends in D

explanation.surface: A snow leopard at last getting its first teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snow leopard' reads as one animal, but the definition is 'Snow' alone. 'cutting' puts D, the last of leopard, inside POWER.
explanation.definitionFit: Powder is fresh, dry, fine snow, as skiers call it.

clue.text: Supporter beginning to sing Flower of Scotland

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is the letter it opens with, so only that first character comes across.

parts.note: the opening letter of sing
the Tay is Scotland's longest river, and a river is a thing that flows

explanation.surface: A supporter in the crowd striking up the Scottish anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the crossword's oldest pun — not a bloom but a flow-er, a thing that flows — and the italics on the anthem's title keep you singing rather than looking at rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporter → STAY: a stay is the rope or brace that holds a mast up, and stays are the stiffening in a corset.

clue.text: Car men possibly needing welding ring AA

indicators.note: 'Possibly' warns that what precedes is one instance of the answer's category rather than a synonym for the whole of it.
Welding fuses separate pieces into a single object, so the chunks are run together in the order given.

parts.note: a ring is a circle, and a circle is the shape of that letter
the first of the two letters is read as the word a, which means per — five pounds a head is five pounds per head — while the second stays as it is

explanation.surface: Mechanics with a welding job on their hands calling out the motoring breakdown service.
explanation.walkthrough: Bizet's Carmen is both the trap and the point: two words on the page, one work in the ear. The AA is a breakdown service only in the surface story.
explanation.definitionFit: Car men → OPERA: run together it is Bizet's Carmen, and 'possibly' flags that one named work is standing in for the art form.

clue.text: Hardcore fans frequently very forgiving?

parts.note: ultras are football's most fervent supporters, the ones who organise the chanting
oft is the poetic short form of often

explanation.surface: Football's most fanatical supporters turning out to be remarkably easy-going.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last two words, and they go on sounding like more talk about football supporters, so the sentence never seems to change subject. An S changes sides between the two readings.
explanation.definitionFit: very forgiving → ULTRASOFT: 'soft' in the sense of lenient, as in soft on offenders, with 'ultra' doing the work of 'very'.

clue.text: Misuse of tacky tape in Yankees' game

indicators.note: Misusing something is handling it wrongly, and letters handled wrongly come out in the wrong order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Sticky tape being put to a use it was never meant for at a baseball game.
explanation.walkthrough: The Yankees are Americans in general rather than the New York club, and the game is the hand-clapping nursery rhyme that British children chant as pat-a-cake.
explanation.definitionFit: Yankees’ game → PATTY-CAKE: patty-cake is the American name for the children's clapping game, so 'Yankees'' marks which side of the Atlantic the name comes from.

clue.text: Stuffed thing in underwear

definitions.meaning: the soft bear a child takes to bed, named after President Roosevelt

explanation.surface: Something padded turning up in somebody's underwear drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: One word covers a nursery toy and a piece of lingerie, and the clue runs the two senses into a single phrase so that the join between them disappears.
explanation.definitionFit: A teddy is both the plush bear named after Theodore Roosevelt and a woman's one-piece camisole-and-knickers undergarment.

clue.text: Explorer brought back oddly cool plant

indicators.note: brought back means turned round, so the explorer's name is read backwards

parts.note: John Cabot, the Italian explorer who sailed for England to North America in 1497

indicators.note: oddly means take the odd-numbered letters, the first and third

parts.note: its first and third letters are C and O

explanation.surface: An explorer returned home with a strangely chilled specimen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' reverses CABOT into TOBAC, and 'oddly' takes C and O from cool. Fittingly, tobacco was brought back to Europe by explorers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobacco is the leafy plant Nicotiana, grown for leaves that are dried and smoked.

clue.text: Giveaway on the back of Monopoly set

parts.note: a tell is the unconscious sign that gives a poker player away

indicators.note: The back of a word is where its final letter sits, so that closing character is all that comes across.

parts.note: the last letter of monopolY

explanation.surface: A free gift advertised on the back of a Monopoly box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' sits at the end looking like part of the board-game picture, a Monopoly set, and it is the definition: the box in the corner of the living room.
explanation.definitionFit: set → TELLY: a television receiver is 'the set', and telly is the everyday British word for that same box.

clue.text: Businessmen making a return on people's investment

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the nation follows the other pieces

parts.note: Business is CO (company) and men is OR (other ranks); OR making a return, read backwards, gives RO
a people is a nation; the 's stands for 'is'

explanation.surface: Entrepreneurs earning a profit on the public's money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Businessmen' splits into Business and men, and only the men make a return. 'investment' is not finance: it is the ceremony of investing a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: A coronation is the formal investiture of a monarch with crown and authority, so an investment in that ceremonial sense.

clue.text: Dynasty's leading male produces puzzle

indicators.note: Whatever leads goes in front, so the dynasty's letters are placed ahead of the ones that follow.

parts.note: the Tang ruled China for three centuries
a ram is the male sheep

explanation.surface: The leading man of the glossy American soap leaving everybody baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: A Chinese dynasty and an eighties soap share a word, and the capital D belongs equally to both, so nothing in the sentence points east.
explanation.definitionFit: puzzle → TANGRAM: the Chinese dissection puzzle whose seven flat pieces are rearranged into silhouettes is one particular kind of puzzle.

clue.text: Confused footballer on the radio

indicators.note: A name heard on the radio reaches you as sound alone, so you write down what it sounds like rather than how it is spelt.

parts.note: Lionel Messi, the Argentinian forward, said aloud

explanation.surface: A confused footballer being discussed by commentators on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the spelling moves: the Argentinian's name ends in an I where the adjective ends in a Y, so to the ear the two are identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Confused → MESSY: a messy situation is a muddled and disordered one, so 'confused' names the state of things rather than a state of mind.

clue.text: 1-0 by the end for Manchester City

parts.note: the answer to 1-down is SOAP, and Lux is the long-running brand of it
a written nought is the letter it looks like

indicators.note: The end of a name is its final letter, so only the last character of the town is used.

parts.note: the last letter of ManchesteR

explanation.surface: A one-nil scoreline going Manchester City's way.
explanation.walkthrough: Manchester City is a football club until the two words come apart: 'City' is the definition and Manchester is being asked only for its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: City → LUXOR: the Egyptian city on the Nile, built over the ruins of ancient Thebes, is a city in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Comeback of Twilight mostly a bit of froth

indicators.note: A comeback is a return along the way you came, so the letters are read back to front.
Mostly means most of a thing and not all of it, so the word gives up its final letter.

parts.note: twilight is dusk, and 'mostly' leaves the closing K behind

explanation.surface: The vampire film franchise making a return and being written off as lightweight.
explanation.walkthrough: In italics Twilight is the film series; in plain English it is dusk, and that is the reading the wordplay needs. Setters treat the singular of suds as a fair word.
explanation.definitionFit: a bit of froth → SUD: the singular of suds, one bubble of the soapy foam that a wash raises.

clue.text: Negative director upset Sid Owen

indicators.note: Upsetting something tips its contents out in a heap, and letters tipped out land in a fresh order.

parts.note: d is the credits' short form of director
anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: A film director losing his temper with the actor Sid Owen.
explanation.walkthrough: Sid Owen played Ricky Butcher in EastEnders for two decades, which is why his name turns up in a soap-themed grid, and the clue reads as a row on set.
explanation.definitionFit: Negative → DOWNSIDE: the downside of a plan is its negative, the drawback you weigh against the advantages.

clue.text: Sinner's broken by Norrie at the start and quits

indicators.note: Breaking into something opens it in the middle, so the letter is pushed between the ones already there.

parts.note: Eve was the one who took the fruit in Genesis, and her apostrophe-s comes along with her

indicators.note: The start of a name is the letter it opens with, so only that first character is taken.

parts.note: the first letter of Norrie

explanation.surface: A tennis player broken early on by Norrie and then walking off the court.
explanation.walkthrough: Jannik Sinner and Cameron Norrie are both on the men's tour, which is what keeps the capital S looking like a surname instead of the woman in Eden.
explanation.definitionFit: quits → EVENS: to be quits is to owe nothing either way, and evens is that same level state, the bookmaker's word for a 50-50 chance.

clue.text: Jackie Corkhill finishes fish in fabulous place

indicators.note: finishes means the end letter of each of the two names

parts.note: Jackie Corkhill was a character in the Liverpool soap Brookside; her names end in E and L
the dorado, or mahi-mahi, is a large tropical sea fish

explanation.surface: A soap character's fish dish served in some legendary location.
explanation.walkthrough: In a puzzle full of soap operas, the answer was also a short-lived BBC soap. E and L end the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: El Dorado was the legendary city of gold sought by Spanish conquistadors, a place existing only in fable.

clue.text: Father working in old juvenile training pants

indicators.note: 'In' puts one thing inside another, so the letters before it are dropped into the middle of what follows.

parts.note: the Youth Training Scheme, the British programme that took school-leavers through the 1980s and was wound up in 1990
Fr is how a priest's title is written in front of his name
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A priest employed on a defunct government scheme for training young people.
explanation.walkthrough: A whole institution is compressed into three letters here, and 'old' is the setter's way of saying the scheme no longer exists rather than a word about age.
explanation.definitionFit: pants → Y-FRONTS: pants is the British word for underpants, and Y-fronts are the men's briefs with the Y-shaped seam at the front.

clue.text: Hamburg's endless winding steps

indicators.note: winding means twisting and turning, so the remaining letters are rearranged
endless means the city's name loses its last letter

parts.note: the German port city of Hamburg; the 's stands for 'is'

explanation.surface: A spiralling staircase in the German port city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' takes G off HAMBURG, and 'winding' rearranges HAMBUR into the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhumba is a ballroom dance of Cuban origin, a set of dance steps.

clue.text: Seat deals flying with Delta

indicators.note: Things sent flying scatter and land anyhow, which is what becomes of these letters.

parts.note: anagram fodder, five letters
Delta is D in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: Cheap airline seats going on sale with Delta.
explanation.walkthrough: Delta is an airline in the surface and a single letter in the wordplay, and that swap is what the clue turns on; the seat is a horse's or a bicycle's.
explanation.definitionFit: Seat → SADDLE: the seat a rider sits on, whether strapped to a horse's back or bolted to a bicycle frame.

clue.text: Spooner's cash balance when things may be on the line?

definitions.text: when things may be on the line?

indicators.note: Spooner's signals swapping the opening sounds of two words, after the Reverend Spooner

parts.note: dosh is British slang for cash
to balance is to weigh, as on scales

explanation.surface: A financial question about a balance of money at risk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooner's' swaps the opening sounds of DOSH and WEIGH to say 'wosh day', how British speakers say the answer. 'on the line' means hung on the washing line, not at risk.
explanation.definitionFit: Washday was the household's set day for laundry, when washed clothes hung outside to dry.

clue.text: Nothing stops fair contest

indicators.note: To stop a gap is to plug it, so the letter is pushed into the middle of the word beside it.

parts.note: a just decision is a fair one
nothing is written as a nought, which is that letter's shape

explanation.surface: Nothing standing in the way of a fair fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing stops fair' reads as a single phrase about there being no obstacle, and all three words are wordplay. The contest is the one knights fought with lances.
explanation.definitionFit: contest → JOUST: the lance-to-lance charge between two mounted knights is a contest, and the word still covers any head-to-head duel.

clue.text: Young Australian's delight catching English opener

indicators.note: Catching something holds it inside your grasp, so the letter is trapped in the middle of the word.

parts.note: joy is delight, and it opens up to take a letter

indicators.note: The opener of a word is the letter that opens it, so only that first character is used.

parts.note: the first letter of English

explanation.surface: An Australian fielder's glee at catching England's opening batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the cricket picture is complete — a catch, an opener, an Australian celebrating — and the answer is a kangaroo's young.
explanation.definitionFit: Young Australian → JOEY: the young of a kangaroo or other marsupial, Australian by species rather than by nationality.

clue.text: Expelled inspectors embarrassed outside pub

indicators.note: What stands outside goes round the outside, so the pub is enclosed by the two pieces on either side of it.

parts.note: DI is the police rank detective inspector, and the clue asks for more than one
an embarrassed face goes red
the bar is the counter a pub serves its drinks over

explanation.surface: Detectives going red in the face outside a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The pub in the middle is the same bar a barrister is called to, which is why being stripped of it amounts to expulsion from the profession.
explanation.definitionFit: Expelled → DISBARRED: a barrister struck off is expelled from the bar, so the general word covers this one particular expulsion.

clue.text: Defaced information book

definitions.note: The answer ends in S but names one thing: the Acts of the Apostles is a single book, so a singular definition is right.

indicators.note: Take the face off a word and its front letter goes, which is the reading 'de-faced' is asking for.

parts.note: facts are information, and this is the word about to lose its face

explanation.surface: A reference book that somebody has scribbled all over.
explanation.walkthrough: Acts of the Apostles is a New Testament book, so 'book' defines by example. 'Defaced' works twice over: a vandalised volume in the surface, a beheaded word in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: book → ACTS: the Acts of the Apostles is one of the books of the New Testament, named here by its category.

clue.text: Prepared food for heart-throb

definitions.meaning: a course as it reaches the table, cooked and plated
slang for a strikingly good-looking person

explanation.surface: Somebody cooking a meal for the object of their affections.
explanation.walkthrough: Food on the table and food for the eye: the same word covers a plated course and a person worth staring at, and 'for' pretends to be a preposition of purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish is both a prepared course served at table and, in slang, a person good-looking enough to stop traffic.

clue.text: Dorothy's aunt and British drunk get involved

parts.note: Auntie Em brought Dorothy up on the Kansas farm in The Wizard of Oz
Br is the standard short form of British
someone well oiled has had far too much to drink

explanation.surface: Dorothy's aunt getting mixed up with a drunken Brit.
explanation.walkthrough: Well-oiled is British slang for thoroughly drunk, and Auntie Em is Dorothy's guardian on the Kansas farm; the clue introduces two people who have never met.
explanation.definitionFit: involved → EMBROILED: to be embroiled is to be caught up in a quarrel or a mess, the sense of 'involved' that carries trouble with it.

clue.text: Main movements of Mendelssohn's 4th introduced by strings

indicators.note: The 4th of a name is the letter standing in fourth place when you count from the front of it.

parts.note: ties are strings for fastening, as on an apron

indicators.note: To introduce something is to bring it inside, so the strings take the letter into the middle of themselves.

parts.note: the fourth letter of menDelssohn

explanation.surface: The principal movements of Mendelssohn's Fourth Symphony, opened by the string section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the old word for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main, so the movements are the sea's. Mendelssohn's Fourth is the Italian Symphony, which keeps you in the concert hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Main movements → TIDES: 'main' is the poetic name for the open sea, and the tides are the regular movements of it.
